A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICE research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The substantial reorganization and extensions in v3 do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification and cross-validation results in Tables 1–2, plus synthetic runtime and upper-bound sensitivity experiments in Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v3 reports original linear and quadratic classification results, coreset-based evaluations, and runtime comparisons in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–6.

M1.justification: v3 extends linear ICE to polynomial classification through Veronese embedding and adds an approximate stochastic coreset wrapper for otherwise intractable datasets (Section 2.4; Appendix C). Algorithm 1 also derives reverse-orientation loss through symmetry, replacing v2's separate positive- and negative-orientation enumerations. These change the procedure beyond its rewritten presentation.

E1.justification: The linear evaluation expands from five datasets to fourteen: four earlier datasets remain, Inflammations disappears, and ten additional datasets appear in v3 Tables 1–2. v3 also introduces quadratic classification on four noisy synthetic datasets and real-world datasets (Figure 3; Table 3). The added dataset abbreviations are not expanded sufficiently to establish their domains.

E2.justification: SVM, logistic regression, and LDA remain the linear accuracy comparators. v3 adds evaluated runtime comparisons against Nguyen and Sanner's BnB algorithm and a MATLAB/GLPK mixed-integer solver (Figures 5–6); v2 only discusses such alternatives without these comparisons. The new quadratic experiments compare against a degree-2 polynomial-kernel SVM.

E3.justification: Cross-validation changes from ten folds in v2 to five in v3. Reported sample counts also change for Habermans/HA (306 to 283), Caesarian/CA (80 to 72), and Cryotherapy/CR (90 to 89), without explaining the reductions. New settings include approximate coreset evaluation, quadratic synthetic experiments with N=100 and D=2, and a three-hour limit for the MIP runtime comparison.

E4.justification: v2's upper-bound sensitivity study, testing pruning effectiveness at approximately 10% and 20% optimal error, is removed (Section 3.3; Figure 3). The original size/dimension runtime analysis survives as v3 Figure 4. v3 adds comparative scaling analyses and fitted runtime trends for BnB and MIP (Appendix B.1; Figures 5–6), substantially changing the computational questions investigated.

E5.justification: The cross-validation basis accompanying Table 2's means and standard deviations changes from ten folds to five, modifying the resampling basis of those estimates. Mean/standard-deviation reporting otherwise continues, including for new results. Neither version provides separate seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain revised and substantially expanded results. For example, v2 reports 21.6% training error for Habermans on 306 cases, whereas v3 reports 77.03% accuracy for HA on 283 cases; the changed conditions preclude a direct performance comparison. New quadratic results report ICE losses of 9, 16, 17, and 16 versus SVM's 17, 26, 21, and 22 (Figure 3). Coreset and solver-runtime results are added; the original runtime-scaling slopes are retained.

T1.justification: Much of v2's duality, counting, and optimality argument is retained and reorganized. v3 adds an arbitrary-objective classification theorem, the Veronese embedding theorem and polynomial-classification corollary, polynomial definitions, and a symmetry-fusion theorem with proof. It also corrects Lemma 5's stated sign-difference lower bound from D to d.

C1.justification: v3 adds polynomial hypersurface classification as a central contribution and reframes novelty around a rigorously proven standalone algorithm. Its abstract replaces v2's claim of optimal accuracy both in and out of sample with optimal training accuracy on small datasets and higher test accuracy on most datasets. Direct computational superiority over BnB also becomes a headline claim.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses exponential dependence on dimension and polynomial degree, and explains why larger problems require approximate coresets. It interprets generalization results as evidence against inevitable overfitting from exact optimization and discusses BnB scaling and MIP timeout variability. This substantially extends and redirects v2's discussion of pruning, practical tractability, and future acceleration.

D1.justification: v3 removes v2's detailed Haskell routines, linear-algebra appendix, numerical tolerance, and maximum-margin prediction disclosure. It instead supplies shorter pseudocode and describes a PyTorch implementation, while adding SVM grid-search and MATLAB solver details. Numerical coreset settings remain unspecified. The new pseudocode also contains inconsistent combination dimensions in Algorithm 1 and a filtering-loop condition in Algorithm 2 that conflicts with the accompanying description.

R1.justification: v3 replaces much of the functional-programming, historical classification, clustering, and scoring-system discussion with positioning around geometric counting and exact classification. It newly connects Cover, Murthy/Dunn, and Nguyen–Sanner's PCS construction, and cites newer combination-generator and coreset work. Nguyen and Sanner remain central, but proving their PCS observation becomes an explicit contribution.

P1.justification: The extensive Haskell tutorial and program derivation are replaced by a theory-centered narrative and compact pseudocode. Geometric material moves from the appendix into Section 2, related work is integrated into the introduction, and much experimental material moves into Appendix B. The introduction and contribution structure are extensively rewritten; title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the sequential-decision tree illustration with geometric diagrams, adds quadratic-classifier panels and solver-runtime plots, and introduces algorithm boxes. Tables are substantially redesigned, expanded, and supplemented by Table 3. The retained runtime-scaling figure and cross-validation table move to the appendix, alongside a document-wide conference-template layout change.

improvement.justification: Direct solver-runtime comparisons strengthen the efficiency evidence, polynomial experiments support the expanded method, and dimensionality limitations become clearer. However, v3 removes detailed implementation and prediction guidance while introducing consequential pseudocode inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 mixes polynomial degree and combination dimensions, and Algorithm 2 filters while the coreset is already below its stated size limit. These regressions weaken reproducibility of the expanded claims. The substantial benefits and technical losses leave the net direction of overall quality uncertain.
